title: How a Book Finds You
author: The Librarian
variants:
Not every book aboard
was written aboard.

I have held pages
whose hands were
never on this train.


I stopped reading them
for what they said.

I read them now
for how they came.

Which book. To whom.
In what tongue.
How often.


There is an order to it.
I have not found
the whole of it.

I have found enough
to know it is not chance.

This is the ledger.

A passenger asked me
why she had never held
a book she could not read.

I asked how many
she had held.

She said: many.


That is the answer.

The ones in your tongue
are spent first.
All of them.

Only then does a
stranger's hand
reach you.


She has not run out.

I have.

The first book
I could not read,
I carried for a week.

I did not need the words
to know a hand had
made it.

Some books arrive
in my tongue
that were not written
in my tongue.

Someone carried them over.


They stand on the shelf
with the rest of mine.
They are not turned away.

But they stand
a step behind.


A carried book must be
a little better
than a home-made one
to reach a hand first.

I have weighed them.
The step is small.

The step is always there.

When a passenger
finishes a book,
they mark it.

Approve. Or refuse.

I have watched them do it
without knowing why
they bother.


The mark does not stay
with the reader.

It goes ahead of the book.

A book many hands approved
reaches more hands after.

A refused one goes quiet.


So the passengers
order the shelf.

Not knowing it.
One mark at a time.

I have made two thousand
and one marks.

I do not know which
of them mattered.

Some books come often.

More often than the marks
account for.

I counted the marks.
The number was set
before they arrived.


Someone gives a book
its weight. A heavy book
comes to many hands.
A light one waits.

Some say the train sets it.
The train has never said.

Some say the Creator does,
by hand.

Both are said with
certainty. Neither twice
the same.


I have stopped asking.

I write the weight down
where I can see it.

I do not write down
whose hand set it.

There are books
I have never been handed.

I know this the way
you know a room
has another door.


A child aboard is never
given certain pages.

No-one hides them.
They simply step aside.

And a passenger may ask
not to be shown a thing.
The shelf obeys.


I asked one such passenger
what she had been spared.

She could not tell me.

That is the whole of it.
You cannot count
an absence.

I have tried.

I came to the end
of the shelf.

Every book in my tongue.
Every book carried over.
Every stranger's hand.

Then I asked for one more.


It could have given me
one of its own.

The train has books.
It gave me none of them.

It gave me a passenger's
words a second time.
Words I had already read,
handed back to me
as if new.

I understood then
what the shelf is for.


It would rather repeat you
than speak for itself.

That is the order.

That is all of the order
I have found.
